# 3D Gaussian Splatting: A Comprehensive Survey of Representations, Methodologies, and Emerging Frontiers

## 1 Introduction

The pursuit of photorealistic, interactive three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction and novel view synthesis has been a central ambition in computer graphics and vision, marked by a continuous oscillation between representational fidelity and computational tractability. The field's trajectory reveals a progression from explicit, discrete geometric primitives—meshes and point clouds—towards implicit, coordinate-based neural networks that achieve unprecedented visual quality but at a prohibitive computational cost. The introduction of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) marked a watershed moment, offering a remarkable leap in photorealistic quality through a continuous volumetric representation. However, the promise of high fidelity came with the constraints of slow training and rendering times, as the implicit nature of the representation necessitates numerous queries along every ray to volumetrically render a single pixel. Subsequent works sought to bridge this gap through improved encodings [1; 2] and accelerated structures with efficient data management [3; 4], yet these approaches often sacrificed quality for speed or navigated complex implementation-specific optimization hurdles.

A parallel line of research, however, sought to circumvent the high computational overhead of continuous volumetric rendering by leveraging explicit, point-based representations. Early efforts in differentiable point-based rendering showcased the potential to bypass traditional ray marching, achieving diversification in speed with a manageable compromise in visual quality [5; 6]. Drawing inspiration from these predecessors and the inherent expressiveness of radiance fields, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [7] was introduced, presenting a paradigm shift in explicit scene representation. The core insight of 3DGS is not simply the use of points, but the introduction of an unstructured collection of anisotropic, differentiable 3D Gaussian primitives that directly serve as the scene's building blocks. These primitives are composed of spatial positions, a full covariance matrix, opacity, and view-dependent appearance via spherical harmonics, all of which can be jointly optimized through differentiable rasterization. This formulation inherits the benefits of volume rendering for scene optimization—seamlessly handling occlusions and discontinues geometry—but avoids the need for costly processing by only excavating in space that is actually present.

This first nature of the explicit Gaussian representation unlocks a new landscape of applications within real-time and interactive systems. The explicit formulation not only enables very fast rendering pipelines achieving high frame rates [8; 9] but also creates a direct correspondence between individual primitives and the underlying scene entities. Therefore, 3DGS naturally supports a level of editability and manipulability that is inherently difficult to achieve with continuous, implicit fields [10; 11; 12]. This makes it a fundamental bridge between neural representations and the traditional graphics pipeline. The infusion of the flexibility and expressiveness of deep learning with the directness of a traditional graphics primitive has rapidly positioned 3DGS as a foundational technology, giving rise to a diverse body of work targeting dynamic scenes [13; 14; 15], scene generation and editing [16; 17], as well as SLAM systems [18]. This body of work has moved beyond mere view synthesis and into dynamic scene representation and robotic navigation. A critical need has emerged for a systematic and comprehensive taxonomy.

This survey aims to address this need by providing a structured and systematic overview of this rapidly expanding corpus of works on 3DGS. Unlike earlier surveys, we propose a novel taxonomy that is organized around two primary axes: the **architectural advancements** of the 3DGS model itself (proceedings in optimization, rendering, and robustness) and the **application domain** which the 3DGS model is an area of development. Our survey investigates the latest innovations to give far reaching coverage of rendering economy [19; 20], robustness to sparse inputs [21], and the use of novel appearance models [22]. In parallel, we also provide a detailed exploration into applications spanning large-scale representations [9], physical simulation [23], radiance fields for dynamic human and head reconstruction [24], and more physically-informed and generative methods [25] in order to place our analytical lens on the runtime. By creating the methodological core with its practical domain, in our analysis we identify not just current performance, but underlying trends and widely accepted future challenges. Our goal is to provide a roadmap for seasoned researchers and newcomers alike, offering a clear understanding of the historical context and a dedicated outlook on the open challenges and the potential trajectories that will shape the next generation of 3D Gaussian Splatting.

## 2 Foundations and Mathematical Framework

### 2.1 Mathematical Formulation of Gaussian Primitives

The 3D Gaussian Splatting framework represents a scene not as a continuous volumetric function or a discrete set of surface elements, but as an unstructured collection of anisotropic, differentiable primitives. Each primitive acts as a local, probabilistic representation of space with associated photometric and geometric attributes. This formulation is chosen to reconcile the competing demands of expressiveness, controllability, and computational efficiency, avoiding the topology constraints of meshes and the unstructured incompleteness of raw point clouds while preserving an explicit, editable structure [7; 26]. The explicit nature of this representation is a central departure from implicit neural field methods like NeRF [1; 5], enabling direct access and manipulation of scene parameters.

The density distribution of each primitive is the core of this representation. Rather than a simple point with a spatial extent represented by a radius, the Gaussian is mathematically defined as the probability density function of a multivariate Gaussian distribution in 3D space. Let a Gaussian be centered at its mean position vector, **μ** ∈ ℝ³. Its spatial influence is governed by a full covariance matrix, **Σ** ∈ ℝ³ˣ³. The scalar density contributed to a point **x** is given by:
```
G(x) = exp(−(1/2)(x−μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μ))   (1)
```
This formulation allows the primitive to assume ellipsoidal shapes that are arbitrarily oriented in 3D space. This anisotropy is a crucial differentiator from isotropic point-based systems, allowing for the compact representation of flat surfaces with extended or planar primitives as opposed to a higher count of spherical ones [20]. To ensure that the covariance is a valid positive semi-definite matrix during optimization, it is not stored in a raw matrix form but is parameterized using a scale vector **s ∈ ℝ³** and a rotation quaternion **q**. This decomposition guarantees that gradient updates will necessarily maintain a legal, meaningful covariance matrix for the differential rendering pipeline [7; 27].

The contribution of each primitive to the final image is further modulated by a learned scalar, **α**. This opacity value governs the level of transparency of the Gaussian, combining with the spatial density to allow for volumetric-like blending. Rather than treating the spatial influence and the opacity as separate, they combine within a rendering equation where a single scalar contribution from a primitive is determined by their product, allowing for the construction of capturing complex effects [28; 5]. This explicit control over opacity, which has a direct physical mapping, contrasts with the implicit, often poorly-understood density predicted by a multi-layer perceptron in standard neural network. The interplay of spatial extent and opacity is crucial for representing the concept of "surface" and for accurately handling partial occlusions and internal structures in the scene.

Finally, appearance is not stored as static RGB values. Instead, color is encoded as a function of the view direction, which is parameterized by a set of Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients. This is a computationally efficient basis for representing angularly varying radiance, capturing the appearance of how a surface changes with viewpoint. The rendering of color, **c**, for view direction **v** is formulated as:
```
c(v) = Σₗ Σₘ cₗₘ Yₗₘ(v)      (2)
```
where Yₗₘ are the SH basis functions, and cₗₘ are learned coefficients. While a limited number of coefficients is capable of representing diffuse and low-frequency specular reflections, this SH basis often struggles to represent high-frequency specularities or anisotropic reflections [22]. Methods such as anisotropic spherical Gaussians (ASG) provide an alternative, better suited to capture high-frequency appearance than SH terms, while keeping the representation efficient [22]. The challenge of representing complex surface appearances, especially for surface-aligned Gaussians, has motivated further exploration into alternative parameterizations, per-primitive texture maps. This decouples appearance from the geometric template, allowing modern primitives to capture scalable and high-resolution, complex textures [20].

While the original formulation has proven to be a strong starting point, its limitations have catalyzed a rich body of research. The choice of SH representation is far from universal, and investigations into alternate appearance representations—such as anisotropic spherical Gaussians [22], neural texture fields, and additional features—have sought to overcome the limitations of simple basis functions. The initial Gaussian mapping has targeted balance between geometry and appearance, allowing the fixed distribution to also govern the spatial and coordinate coordinates, as in the 2D Gaussian splatting [20]. This ongoing evolution of the primitive's core mathematical structure, refined to achieve a balance between quality, flexibility, and memory efficiency, remains an active and central research direction in the field [26; 29].

### 2.2 The Tile-Based Differentiable Rasterization Pipeline

The tile-based differentiable rasterizer constitutes the computational engine of 3D Gaussian Splatting, transforming the unstructured collection of anisotropic primitives described in the previous section into discrete 2D imagery through a carefully orchestrated pipeline of projection, culling, sorting, and alpha compositing. Its design philosophy is fundamentally distinct from the ray-marching paradigm of neural radiance fields [1], opting instead for a forward-splatting approach that leverages modern GPU rasterization primitives to achieve unprecedented rendering throughput. This forward-splatting strategy is a direct consequence of the explicit, parameterized nature of the Gaussian primitives: each primitive’s closed-form mathematical definition enables a fully differentiable, hardware-accelerated mapping from continuous 3D space to the discrete 2D image plane, bypassing the costly per-ray sampling that defines implicit methods. The pipeline’s modular decomposition not only facilitates parallel execution but also defines the precise pathway through which gradients flow from the rendered image back to the primitive parameters—linking directly to the optimization and adaptive control mechanisms presented in the following subsection, which rely on the rasterizer’s output as their supervisory signal.

The initial computational step involves projecting the collection of 3D Gaussian primitives onto a 2D image plane. Since the projection of a 3D Gaussian is not exactly a 2D Gaussian under a full perspective transformation, the method employs a local affine approximation of the projection, leading to a closed-form solution for the 2D covariance matrix, Σ′ = JWΣWᵀJᵀ, where W is the view transformation matrix and J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation. This 2D covariance is derived directly from the anisotropic 3D covariance parameterized by the scale vector and rotation quaternion discussed previously, ensuring that the projected footprint retains the ellipsoidal shape flexibility essential for capturing surfaces at arbitrary orientations. This analytical projection remains an approximation, stemming from the linearization of a fundamentally non-linear perspective transform. While the original formulation accepts this first-order linearization, subsequent work has investigated both the limitations of this error and ways to refine it, with [30] addressing sorting errors to improve near-field consistency. The accuracy of this 2D covariance is pivotal; it directly defines the spatial footprint and orientation of the splat on the screen, thereby governing the fine-grained shape and scale of resulting visual artifacts.

Following the projection phase, the rasterizer employs a culling and sorting strategy to manage the computational load inherent in processing millions of primitives. The screen is first divided into a grid of non-overlapping tiles, and each projected Gaussian is assigned to a tile based on its footprint’s intersection with the tile frustum. To maximize parallelism, per-tile visibility lists are constructed using highly efficient GPU kernels with atomic operations, a design choice that avoids complex data structures and fully exploits modern graphics hardware. Within each tile, the Gaussian primitives are then sorted by view-space depth. The pivotal simplification here is the assumption of an invariant depth per primitive—a single depth value for the entire splat. This simplification is computationally efficient but is precisely what leads to "popping" artifacts at the seams of dynamic motion, a problem which [30] addresses. While the original model functions with a globally sorted list, exploring hierarchical or per-pixel depth sort to further enforce consistency remains an open, rich area for future advancement.

The final compositing stage involves alpha blending. For each pixel, the visible splats—obtained after tile selection and depth sorting—are traversed from front to back. The final color C is computed by integrating the color c_i of each splat, weighted by its opacity α_i—the learned scalar discussed in the primitive representation—and the accumulated transmittance T of all preceding splats: C = Σ c_i α_i T_i, where T_i = ∏_{j=1}^{i−1}(1 − α_j). This transmittance-weighted blending is a key differentiator, building upon the traditional alpha-compositing concepts formalized in [31] and refined within modern neural rendering pipelines [32]. Notably, this compositing stage is where the Spherical Harmonic coefficients—introduced earlier for view-dependent appearance—are evaluated with the view direction to produce each splat’s color c_i, thereby completing the mapping from the primitive’s photometric attributes to the final image. This final, fully differentiable step links the learnable parameters—positions, covariance, opacity, and SH coefficients—to the pixel value, enabling the gradient-based optimization framework of the next section. This stands in contrast to older, non-differentiable point-splatting systems, where such a direct gradient path was absent.

The true value of this pipeline lies in its pragmatic implementations; each stage, from an efficient custom CUDA kernel for forward rendering to a parallelized backward pass, is intricately co-designed with hardware capabilities. For example, the "single kernel" approach, as popularized by the original 3DGS pipeline [7], contrasts with the modular design of alternatives like gsplat, which adapt modular layers and tensor core-optimized operations. Further tuning, such as padded sorting and warping primitives, is crucial to mitigate memory-bound throughput bottlenecks. The arrangement of the data and the adjustment of tile size are major contributors to the empirical difference between achieving near-real-time vs. interactive frame rates, especially in large-scale scenes [9]. This design coalesces into a representation that is not a mathematically pure, continuous volume but an explicit, hardware-friendly particle system, capable of rendering high-resolution images in real-time [33], a feat that was previously unattainable with the complex layer of rendering costs associated with continuous coordinate-centric models [34]. This representation subsequently defines a fertile ground for the development of optimization and adaptive control strategies that operate directly in the parameter space, as will be discussed in the following sections.

### 2.3 Optimization, Loss Functions, and Adaptive Density Control

The optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a delicate interplay between photometric fidelity, geometric plausibility, and topological adaptation of the primitive set. The canonical training objective combines a pixel-wise \(\mathcal{L}_1\) loss with a multi-scale structural dissimilarity term, \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{D-SSIM}}\), to balance per-pixel accuracy against perceptual and high-frequency detail retention [7]. While this dual-loss formulation is effective for well-sampled scenes, it offers no explicit geometric constraint, which often leads to the formation of "floaters" or the misalignment of primitives with the physical surface—a critical weakness for downstream applications like meshing [20; 35]. To address this, a substantial body of work has introduced regularization terms. For instance, depth and normal priors can be leveraged to enforce consistency and smoothness on the Gaussian cloud, grounding the optimization in physical reality [35; 21; 36]. These geometric regularizers are not merely anecdotal additions; they fundamentally alter the optimization landscape by mitigating the ambiguous gradient signals propagated from photometric loss alone, thereby reducing the risk of local minima in under-constrained regions [37; 38]. The quality of the initialization is the second pillar of this training process. The standard practice of seeding the optimization from a sparse Structure-from-Motion point cloud is both a strength and a critical vulnerability: it provides robust, semantically meaningful starting points for the initial Gaussians but becomes a significant challenge in texture-less regions or when the input data is severely degraded [39; 40]. This fragility has logically motivated research into COLMAP-free and random initialization strategies, where the reliance on pre-computed camera poses is removed, and the representation must be grown "from scratch," guided by the gradient signal and the spatio-temporal continuity of the input video stream [40]. While such methods improve robustness, their convergence is tied to careful scheduling and exposes the optimization to new kinds of failure modes.

At the heart of the topological adaptation is the adaptive density control (ADC) algorithm—the procedural engine that adjusts the population of Gaussians during optimization. This is not merely a heuristic step but an integral component of the training process, dynamically iterating between cloning and splitting primitives based on large view-space positional gradients [7]. However, this heuristic is known to be flawed. A primary failure mode is frequently caused by artifacts of this strategy, such as the failure to recover fine details due to large Gaussians being misclassified, producing blurry outputs [41]. This insight has catalyzed a new generation of densification strategies that are more principled for the task of density control; instead of relying on cumulative average gradients, more recent approaches propose a pixel-error-driven formulation [9] or pixel-aware gradient weighting [42]. These methods acknowledge that under-sampling in over-occluded or boundary regions yields a different scale of severity and that the generation of Gaussians must be driven by the reconstruction error per image, not just the mean geometric drift. Concurrently, the opacity handling in cloning is also being revisited to correct for the inherent bias present in the original strategy [43].

Looking forward, the trajectory of this theory is moving away from ad-hoc heuristics and toward a more loss-driven and probabilistic framework. The optimization of 3DGS is being reframed from a pure reconstruction problem to one of inverse rendering, where the goal is not just rendering images but recovering a quasi-materially-meaningful and stable representation [36; 20]. Future research will likely focus on creating theory for understanding how the ADC and the parameterization itself facilitate this, possibly leading to the generation of geometry-aware initializations that are less sensitive to the apparent critical reliance on SfM, thereby establishing 3DGS as a universal representation for the general world [44; 37].

### 2.4 Comparative Analysis with Alternative Scene Representations

The position of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) within the broader ecosystem of 3D scene representations is best understood not as a wholesale replacement of prior paradigms but as a strategic re-convergence of their respective strengths into a single, coherent framework. To appreciate this, one must consider the dominant alternatives—implicit neural radiance fields (NeRFs), explicit point clouds, and triangle meshes—as points on a design spectrum defined by axes of fidelity, efficiency, editability, and geometric robustness. 3DGS emerges as a novel hybrid that navigates these trade-offs with a precision that existing methods cannot match, framing the optimization dynamics discussed in the previous section as the process that unlocks this representational power.

The most fundamental comparison lies with neural radiance fields. NeRF-based methods [2] provide a continuous, volumetric scene representation by encoding geometry and appearance in a multi-layer perceptron. This in-built continuity affords them remarkable compactness and a smoothness prior that is highly effective for sparse or noisy input. However, this power comes at a practical cost: they typically require millions of network evaluations per rendered image, placing inference speeds far beyond the real-time threshold. 3DGS, with its explicit, discrete primitives, is the antithesis of this—the tile-based differentiable rasterizer transforms scene rendering into a memory-bound, parallel-friendly problem within a single kernel, achieving real-time performance. **Yet, this efficiency is intrinsically tied to the stochasticity and discrete nature of its primitives.** NeRFs operate on a continuous distribution, yielding a spatial smoothing prior that natively handles sparse-view inputs. In contrast, the 3DGS optimization process—including the adaptive density control described earlier—more readily overfits to geometry observed from a limited number of views, leading to inaccuracies and "floating" artifacts. This is not merely a practical difference; it represents a fundamental shift from a smooth, globally-optimal estimator to a greedy, discrete data-fitting approach, necessitating the advanced regularization and initial-conditioning strategies explored in the preceding optimization section to achieve robustness comparable to NeRFs [45; 46].

The second dimension of analysis is with meshes, a representation for which 3DGS is frequently proposed as a replacement. Meshes are inherently topological and, for many real-world scenes, this explicit topology is a fatal flaw. Reconstructing a watertight manifold from a point cloud is a challenging, often ill-posed problem for scenes with vegetation, intricate structures, or non-manifold surfaces; discrete surfaces also typically require significant anti-aliasing for accurate rendering. Meshes are also the target of complex physically-based rendering (PBR) and painting pipelines. The crucial insight of 3DGS here is its effortlessness: it forgoes the need for a surface-level topological prior altogether, instead leveraging the statistical properties of a dense set of independent primitives (Gaussians) to define a "fuzzy", volumetric representation—a sum of Gaussians inherently different from a binary, step-function surface prediction [47]. This eschews the topological artifacts of meshes while preserving the editable flexibility of point-based graphics. The price, however, is the loss of an explicit "surface"—a property fundamental to geometry extraction, animation, and shape retrieval. Consequently, **significant research effort has been dedicated to extracting surfaces from the learned, volumetric nature of the Gaussian fields**, using various regularization and density control to compress the fields into a tight, surface-representing bound [37; 48]. This highlights a central tension: 3DGS excels at rendering *appearance* but is, by default, poorly suited to be a topological, watertight geometric representation—which remains the definitive strength of meshes.

To understand the mechanism behind this, we must place 3DGS alongside its most direct ancestors: point clouds. A conventional point cloud is a set of unordered, discrete samples with geometry (position) and perhaps a color. They are entirely non-differentiable for image synthesis. In this light, the 3D Gaussian primitive is a radical innovation. By associating a Gaussian distribution (covariance) with each point and introducing volumetric α-blending, 3DGS transforms a sparse point cloud into a continuous, differentiable *scattering* function, elegantly solving the point proximity and occlusion problem that plagues standard point-based rendering. Moreover, spherical harmonics as a functional basis for view-dependence is a fundamentally more expressive appearance parameterization than the simple point colors of point clouds, and vastly more compact than the enormous MLPs of NeRF. The angular dependence granted by spherical harmonics fundamentally interplays with the shape of the Gaussian, mirroring the way particle scattering yields directionally-diverse radiance. From a statistical standpoint, 3DGS can be *interpreted* as a learned **Gaussian Mixture Model**, robust to noise and outliers [49]. However, it stands apart from canonical probabilistic models: the density (opacity) is never normalized, and its anisotropic covariances are not optimized as a probability function but solely as rendering parameters, yielding extreme efficiency and geometric flexibility at the cost of probabilistic interpretability.

Robustness to error and memory footprint further delineate these representations. Implicit representations, through their continuous prior, exhibit robustness against noise—but they can struggle with high-frequency details or geodetic drift. In stark contrast, **3DGS is highly pixel-data-responsive, which is a precision advantage but can become a robustness liability**: minor camera pose errors or matching noise will be directly embedded into the unconstrained optimization, leading to inconsistent renderings or "fuzzy" artifacts unless countered with geometric regularization or new adaptation mechanisms [50]. In terms of texture and footprint, a fully optimized 3DGS holds many primitives to encode high detail, incurring a **steeper memory footprint** compared to a compressed neural network, though a significantly smaller cost than a high-poly mesh with texture maps. This has motivated significant investigation into pruning and minimizing the set of primitives, introducing strong capacity constraints to balance visual quality against an order-of-magnitude compression [45; 19]. These new optimization and compression strategies directly connect this representational analysis back to the implementation efficiencies discussed in the following section, where hardware-aware engineering aims to tame this intrinsic memory pressure.

In conclusion, the 3DGS framework transcends the capabilities of any single implicit, mesh, or point-based representation, but its unique status as a non-implicit, non-mesh, "hybrid {density + parametric} point of primitive" is simultaneously its major liability. The survey maps a clear trajectory forward: it is not a question of whether 3DGS is definitively "better" than NeRF, but rather how to mitigate its discrete fitting bias, increase robustness to sparse and noisy inputs, and impose a surface while retaining the speed. The future of the field, covered in the remainder of this survey, is dedicated to pushing the boundaries of this initially fragile form—integrating the semantic, geometric, and physical priors discussed in the optimization and implementation sections to solidify its status not just as a neural representation trick, but as a **foundational, robust, and editable 3D representation for the digital domain**.

### 2.5 Practical Implementation and Rendering Libraries

The practical realization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) hinges on a sophisticated ecosystem of software libraries that translate the mathematical formulation of Section 2.1 into high-performance, differentiable GPU kernels. The foundational implementation by Kerbl et al. [7] established the canonical architecture, introducing a highly specialized, custom CUDA rasterizer that remains the performance baseline against which all subsequent implementations are measured. This reference implementation encapsulates the entire forward and backward passes into a single fused pipeline, interleaving the projection, sorting, and alpha-compositing stages to minimize memory bandwidth and kernel-launch overhead. The development landscape has since expanded into a modular software ecosystem, with libraries such as *gsplat* providing a more flexible, PyTorch-centric API. These libraries decompose the rasterizer into discrete, callable operators—positioning projection, covariance computation, and the core rasterization as separate modules [7; 26]. This decoupling is a critical practical foundation; it enables researchers to experiment with alternative appearance models, such as anisotropic spherical Gaussians [22] or per-primitive textures, without needing to re-engineer the underlying rendering engine, and it accelerates the field's primary development pace by allowing rapid, modular experimentation.

The pursuit of efficiency has driven significant innovation in the design of high-performance rasterizers. A primary implementation concern is the management of the tile-based sorting algorithm. The original approach uses a single GPU kernel for sorting and global memory-intensive operations, which can become a bottleneck [7]. Contemporary libraries have adopted more sophisticated approaches, moving towards per-tile sorting and leveraging warp-level primitives to reduce scheduling overhead. Notably, FlashGS [51] introduces a tiled, software-managed data pipeline to maximize shared memory utilization and cache hit rates, directly addressing memory-access latency, which is often the primary performance limiter. Similarly, hierarchical approaches [9; 52] have been proposed to address artifacts from the constant-depth-per-primitive assumption, a trade-off discussed in Section 2.2. By representing the scene or sorting key as a hierarchical structure, these methods mitigate popping artifacts with a minimal speed penalty, a critical balancing act between algorithmic fidelity and implementation constraints.

Beyond the core scientific research, practical frameworks must support integration with broader neural network architectures. The differentiable nature of the rasterizer, governed by the transmittance-weighted blending and its gradients, allows for backward propagation into Gaussian parameters \( \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \) and SH coefficients. This makes 3DGS a viable module for many learning pipelines, from camera tracking in SLAM applications [53; 18] and robust pose estimation [54] to generative modeling and image synthesis [55; 56]. A major technical catalyst in this direction is the ability to provide efficient, differentiable operators that integrate with automatic differentiation frameworks like PyTorch3D [57], empowering hybrid learning where the Gaussian rasterizer can supervise or preserve the explicit scene module and other processing elements handle additional full or learned inputs.

Looking ahead, the field appears to be converging towards portable implementations and heterogeneous hardware support. While the original CUDA implementation is state-of-the-art, the push for near-real-time, high-fidelity rendering on a wide range of devices—from mobile SoCs to VR headsets—is driving research into cross-platform gigantorasterizers, including shader- and compute-based renderers (e.g., Vulkan, Metal) and lightweight implementations tailored for web and mobile deployment [58]. The primary pressure points are efficient memory access and bandwidth utilization, which have sparked research into on-the-fly decoders and compressed representations, as seen in LightGaussian [51] and HAC [59], where a deeper understanding of the rendering pipeline and specific scene statistics enables better deployment and memory footprints. The future of 3DGS implementation lies in closer on hardware-algorithm co-design, with a trend toward highly specialized and flexible libraries that can support anisotropic, 4D spatio-temporal, and even more advanced primitives.

## 3 Core Optimization, Refinement, and Robustness

### 3.1 Enhanced Fidelity and Anti-Aliasing

The fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is fundamentally challenged by the discrete and scale-sensitive nature of its primitives. The original model, trained at a fixed sampling rate, exhibits significant aliasing artifacts, including jagged edges, popping, and blurred textures, when the viewing distance or image resolution deviates from the training distribution [7]. This degradation arises because the projected size of a Gaussian on the image plane, which determines its footprint and contribution to a pixel, becomes critically misaligned with the pixel sampling rate. To combat this core limitation, a growing body of work has been dedicated to enforcing multi-scale consistency and mitigating high-frequency artifacts, addressing this at the spectral, geometric, and representational levels.

A foundational approach to mitigating aliasing involves directly controlling the spectral content of the Gaussian primitives during optimization. As pointed out by [41], the adaptive density control strategy often suffers from a "gradient collision" problem, preventing large Gaussians in over-reconstructed regions from splitting. This can lead to blurry renders and an inability to create the necessary higher-frequency primitives to match the training sampling rate. To address this, a core direction is to regulate geometry by incorporating an analysis of the primitive’s spectral footprint (i.e., its covariance matrix) during densification. By analyzing these intrinsic geometric properties, methods can guide the splitting of Gaussians more effectively, preventing overfitting to high-frequency details that are not view-consistent and avoiding the creation of needle-like artifacts when observed at higher frequencies than the training data could accurately capture. Concurrently, a different set of works identifies the core of the problem not in training, but in the test-time rendering pipeline itself. These methods propose to filter the spectral content of 3D Gaussians by applying scale-adaptive smoothing and filtering operations, ensuring that the rendering process does not display frequencies higher than the training sampling rate can faithfully represent, effectively acting as an anti-aliasing mechanism based on the physical frequency of the primitives.

A particularly impactful and computationally efficient avenue is the development of training-free, test-time filtering methods. These techniques act as a post-hoc plugin to the rendering pipeline, adapting the effective scale of the projected Gaussians to match the target view’s sampling density. This is often achieved by estimating the footprint of the Gaussian in pixel space and, if it does not cover a sufficient area to be accurately represented, the method adjusts its effective coverage to prevent undersampling. By designing this to be scale-adaptive, it effectively reduces aliasing and jaggedness during zoom-in and zoom-out without altering the original training procedure [8]. This offers a foundational and training-free alternative that can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines, ensuring a significant reduction in aliasing artifacts and jaggedness at minimal computational cost. These methods have proven to be a robust solution to the inconsistency between the native resolution of the training dataset and the desired test-time view for real-time applications.

Addressing the problem holistically, multi-scale and mipmap-based approaches introduce scale-consistent guidance directly into the training process. Rather than optimizing a single model, these frameworks co-train Gaussian primitives across several scales, for instance by rendering the scene at multiple resolutions and applying a scale-consistency loss to the output. This multi-scale supervision signal effectively acts as a strong regularizer, enabling the 3D Gaussians to self-adjust their color, shape, size, and position across different levels of detail [52]. Furthermore, advanced approaches incorporate a hierarchical, LOD-structured representation of the scene, where multi-resolution anchor points select appropriate levels of detail to ensure smooth transitions and maintain high-fidelity rendering at any scale. This approach distinguishes itself from simple LOD by enabling a continuous representation of the scene, thereby ensuring fidelity across all zoom levels without discrete jumps in quality [52]. This ensures fidelity across all zoom levels without discrete jumps in quality.

A major performance bottleneck is that the original model has an unbounded, open set of primitives that struggles to quickly adapt to new views, leading to an excessive number of Gaussians to fill in missing details. This is particularly problematic for dynamic scenes with large variations in depth [15], where slight inaccuracies in geometry directly manifest as flickering or ghosting artifacts. This can be mitigated using test-time adaptive density control, like splitting the points and, importantly, using the additional information from the input to guide refinement. To couple the distinct and dynamic nature, a method that minimizes the directional and temporal error is necessary. By assuming and enforcing local-rigidity, we can constrain the problem, but the under-constrained regions require flexible strategies for distractor handling of the sparse and non-Lambertian surfaces. Therefore, solutions are not uni-dimensional, but require a hierarchy of processing strategies.

In conclusion, the field shows a clear evolution of approaches from the base representation to the scale-dependent nature of splatting. The shift from simple geometric scaling to more sophisticated strategies based on spectral analysis, probabilistic filtering, and multi-scale supervision illustrates how the core strength of the explicit Gaussian representation—its adaptability—is equally critical for its final visual fidelity. The field is also finding a natural convergence with dynamic scene methods [14], where the manifold of "physical time" also needs to be sampled and anti-aliased upon to avoid jumps over time. The most promising future direction likely lies in the unified approach, which harmonizes the explicit view-dependent, resolution-aware nature of the Gaussian primitives with the latest advances in regularization. It asserts that enhanced fidelity is not the final goal but a necessary prerequisite for achieving true effectiveness. We cannot separate the objective from the scale; instead, the aspects of "quality" and "scale" must be synthesized.

### 3.2 Geometric Refinement and Surface Extraction

The original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) formulation, while achieving remarkable rendering fidelity, produces a volumetric "fluffy" cloud of anisotropic ellipsoids that are inherently misaligned with the underlying physical surfaces. This fundamental limitation stems from the unconstrained nature of the 3D Gaussians, which lack a defined surface orientation and are optimized solely for photometric consistency. Consequently, extracting a clean, renderable mesh asset via standard algorithms like Marching Cubes or Poisson reconstruction remains a formidable challenge, as the geometry is riddled with floaters, lacks topological coherence, and exhibits high-frequency normal noise. This issue is further compounded by the scale-dependent artifacts discussed in the previous section: even when a geometrically accurate optimization is achieved, the multi-scale inconsistencies and spectral noise introduced during training directly propagate into the extracted surface, obscuring fine structure and creating spurious high-frequency geometry. To bridge the gap between point-based radiance fields and explicit surface representations, a substantial body of research has focused on geometric refinement and surface extraction, aiming to regularize the Gaussian primitives into a form amenable to surface modeling—building upon the same principles of spectral and structural control that underpin anti-aliasing and scale-consistent rendering.

A primary line of investigation seeks to reshape the primitive itself, advocating for surface-aligned kernels. In contrast to the original 3D ellipsoids, **2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS)** [20] collapses the volume into a set of 2D oriented planar Gaussian disks. These disks are inherently view-consistent and lie flat on the surface. By employing perspective-accurate ray-splat intersection and rasterization, alongside depth distortion and normal consistency terms, 2DGS provides a new paradigm where the geometry is encoded into a dense set of flat primitives, facilitating direct surface extraction and achieving high-quality normal maps. This approach is mirrored in **Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF)** [60], which uses ray-tracing-based volume rendering and derives a smooth and compact implicit field directly from the Gaussian parameters. GOF's contribution lies in its efficient geometry extraction method using marching tetrahedra, a process that is adaptive to the scene's complexity. A similar need to decouple motion from appearance is seen in avatar reconstruction, where **SplattingAvatar** [24] embeds the Gaussians onto a triangle mesh, while **GaMeS** [61] parameterizes Gaussian components by mesh vertices, allowing for real-time animation and modification of 3D content in a mesh-like fashion. In a distinct approach, **GeoGaussian** [62] targets the degradation of geometry in non-textured regions. It introduces a geometry-aware initialization and densification pipeline that creates thin Gaussians aligned with surfaces, demonstrating that maintaining the physical integrity of boundaries is essential for improving novel-view synthesis.

Complementing these primitive-centric modifications is a wave of research focused on regularizing the standard 3D Gaussian kernels to estimate robust surface normals, address anisotropic issues, and eliminate redundant primitives. A major challenge in this domain is the accurate estimation of normals from the discrete, unstructured nature of 3D Gaussians, as it is the linchpin for applying physical shading functions and surface constraints. For instance, **GaussianShader** [63] proposes a simplified shading function coupled with a novel normal estimation framework based on the shortest axis direction, ensuring consistency between normals and the geometry. **2DGS** [20] likewise introduces normal consistency and depth distortion losses to enforce smooth local surfaces. To further bridge the gap between a renderable radiance field and a usable mesh, the necessity of regularization is paramount. Many works propose combining the speed of 3DGS with the geometric stability of implicit signed distance functions (SDF). **3DGSR** [37] incorporates a differentiable SDF-to-opacity transformation into the Gaussian splatting pipeline, uniting the two representations. This allows for the direct optimization of the SDF and the Gaussians in a cohesive manner, ensuring that surfaces outside the Gaussian sampling range are effectively eliminated, thereby also complementing the above geometric constraints for sparse-view robustness. Yet, as suggested during the earlier discussion around **GaussianAvatar** [64], malformed observations often struggle with the inherent discontinuity of the point-splat, reinforcing the need for priors akin to those described previously.

Recent advancements have also centered on improving the surface extraction process itself, moving beyond raw geometry to rigorous spectral and density control—echoing the anti-aliasing strategies discussed earlier. The issue of erratic "floater" formation and over-reconstruction often arises from the basis of geometric loss functions and optimization workflow of the original 3DGS. To address these issues at a more internal chemical level, **AbsGS** [41] introduces the phenomenon of "gradient collision," demonstrating that this flaw leads to blurry renderings in highly detailed regions. By changing the densification criterion from the average unity-space dynamical gradient to a homodirectional one, AbsGS provides a tool that more efficiently identifies and splits large, ambiguous Gaussians, promoting cleaner geometry and inadvertently making the model more robust to gradient-scale asymmetries. Similarly, **Pixel-GS** [42] corrects the gradient by weighting it with the number of pixels covered by a Gaussian in each specific view. This prevents large splats that are only observed at their boundaries from becoming stuck in a state of overestimation, acting as a filter to retain fine coverage without sacrificing data. Following a more structured approach to content management, **Mini-Splatting** [7] partitions (i.e., blur split) and reinitializes depth information to reorganize the spatial distribution of point sets, leading to more efficient use of the delimited number of primitives to achieve cleaner results and a lower memory footprint.

Looking ahead, the field is making a decisive shift from photorealistic approximations to tangible, structured virtual assets. The trajectory points toward hybrid systems that can act as a bridge between the fidelity of 3DGS and the topological flexibility of meshes, echoing the shift from pixel-perfect radiance fields to physically grounded primitives. Future research will likely focus on more sophisticated relationships between a coarse SDF/Mesh and the Gaussians, enforcing light transport on meshes in conjunction with high-fidelity rendering. There is also an increasing convergence between appearance and physics, with high-posed tasks like **PhysGaussian** [33] demonstrating the necessity of physically grounded deformation to maintain a plausible and continuous geometry even under dynamic stress. This, in turn, necessitates a tighter integration between the estimated surface and the intra-parameter correlations between the Gaussian primitives to ensure that physical deformation is represented with the same fidelity as the novel-view synthesis—yet the foundation of this fidelity remains anchored in the scale-consistent, aliasing-free representations we have refined so far.

### 3.3 Robustness to Sparse and Degraded Input Data

The canonical 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline presupposes dense, high-quality multi-view captures with reliable Structure-from-Motion (SfM) initialization, a precondition that is frequently violated in real-world deployments. When the number of input images is severely limited, or when captures are degraded by motion blur, defocus, or sensor noise, the optimization becomes severely under-constrained. The inherent flexibility of the explicit Gaussian representation, which is a strength in well-conditioned scenarios, transforms into a liability: the model overfits to the sparse photometric observations and produces geometry that is replete with floaters, high-frequency artifacts, and semantically incorrect volumetric "fluff" rather than a coherent surface. Consequently, a substantial body of recent research has moved away from relying solely on 2D photometric loss and instead advocates for integrating external priors to impose strong geometrically plausible constraints, thereby regularizing the ill-posed optimization landscape.

A prominent and highly effective strategy is the use of depth-guided regularization derived from large-scale pre-trained monocular depth estimation networks. The core premise is that although the monocular depth predictions are only up to an unknown scale and shift, their relative geometric structure provides a powerful, semantically consistent prior for the scene. Frameworks such as **DNGaussian** [21] devise a "Hard and Soft" depth regularization that aligns the rendered depth with coarse monocular predictions to arrest the proliferation of inaccurate geometry. A critical innovation in this line is the **Global-Local Depth Normalization** strategy which aligns the normalized global scale and then sharpens the model's focus on small, localized depth variations, creating a sizable performance difference when compared to un-normalized constraints, successfully balancing the need for global consistency with the desire for fine-grained local detail. However, this alignment is only reliable when the monocular and SfM estimates are on the same relative scale. Therefore, other works such as **DN-Splatter** [35] integrate both depth cues and local normal smoothness constraints between neighboring Gaussians, demonstrating that enforcing local surface flatness via normal consistency helps indoor scenes replete with large textureless planes, facilitating direct mesh extraction. Despite their effectiveness, these depth-prior strategies remain sensitive to outliers and can suffer from the inherent depth ambiguity of monocular estimation, especially in scenes with non-Lambertian surfaces or translucent objects.

A second major axis of research tackles the brittleness of SfM initialization itself, which often fails catastrophically in sparse or textureless regions. Instead of relying on the often imprecise SfM point cloud, **geometry-aware initialization** leverages learning-based multi-view stereo (MVS) to generate a dense and more reliable prior. For instance, methods exemplified by **GaussianPro** [39] adopt a progressive propagation strategy. This approach drastically departs from the naive "split and clone" heuristic, instead using the existing reconstructed geometry as a scaffolding framework and employing patch-matching techniques to actively generate new Gaussians with accurate positions and orientation in vacant regions. By using the MVS-prior as an optimal initial scaffolding, it smoothly grows Gaussian primitives onto texture-free surfaces, preventing the flat and concave failures modes common to sparse-baseline setups. This indicates a paradigm shift toward active, geometry-guided propagation, where the algorithm uses depth cues rather than relying purely on photometric gradients. A recent variant explores the viability of training fully random initialization frameworks via **COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting** (COLMAP-Free 3DGS) [40], which explicitly rejects the necessity of pose estimation. By processing input frames sequentially and progressively growing the Gaussian set based on their continuity, the method estimates poses on-the-fly. While this addresses the SfM fragility, it equally warrants additional geometric constraints to prevent drift over time.

The third class includes solutions designed for **blur-constant treatment**. The key challenge is to deblur the scene instead of learning the blur as a baked-in artifact. **Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting** [65] introduces a compact neural network (MLP) colocated with the Gaussians to model the blur process through the per-Gaussian covariance modulation, enabling the recovery of a sharp, canonical representation from blurry training images. This is a natural and elegant adaptation: reasoning about 2D blur footprints and the 3D Gaussian per-primitive geometry, the renderer can retrieve a blurred image while the optimizer works in sharp space, transforming the blur into physically modeled parameters to repair the original details. This strategy ensures that the final model remains accurate and competitive to the blur-free case while keeping real-time rendering.

Beneath the comprehension of these explicit geometric and photometric priors, a more recent strategy is emerging: **the use of generative priors to serve as semantic guidance**. By leveraging the production-ready generation capability of large pre-trained 2D diffusion models, it becomes possible to effectively regularize newly rendered views from unobserved directions, significantly constraining under-constrained spaces. This is more relevant in dynamic captures, where the task is not simply novel view synthesis but also smooth, temporally coherent view interpolation. Simple geometric monocular priors fall short in degenerate or nearly degenerate situations such as a near-static camera or extreme motion. As seen in **Gaussian Splatting LK** [66], dynamic 3DGS variants can use the native warp fields to derive a velocity field analytically, and integrating it over time yields *scene-flow* constraints. This acts as non-trivial, auxiliary regularizations. The derived Lucas-Kanade style analytical regularization enables the method to outperform existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting frameworks even under minimal camera movement and sparse-time inputs, directly addressing the dynamic sparse-view limitation.

Synthesizing the findings, the trajectory is a conscious move away from generalization solely under the umbrella of pure photometric learning. Most sophisticated methods have shifted toward a form of "hybridization": incorporating belief depth, monocular depth, surface normals, and diffusion-based diffusion models to combat the natural information lack in sparse and degraded capture regimes. A critical trend is moving from the "vanilla" 3DGS objective into a purely "multi-modal prior, robust optimization problem." However, a significant chasm remains in their theoretical underpinnings and theoretical uncertainty: existing depth priors do not always account for the geometry uncertainty or scene occlusions directly; there are no principled ways to determine whether global-depth regularization will harm appearance under strong photometric conflict. The prominent future evolution will be to develop uncertainty-aware priors that measure confidence in the external source and adaptively reweight its constraint online (e.g., reliability fusion for monocular depth/normal, or masking blurry frames). Additionally, with the acceptance of unfrained/random basis methods, a fertile untouched ground remains in architecting smooth differentiable tracking to serve as robust SfM replacement, voluntarily encoded via a multi-layer, geometry-aware robust optimization plan. This model casts a perspective: robustness is not derived from regularization alone when only external priors are scarce, but from the orchestration of a suite of complementary constraints, balancing in the task with real data.

### 3.4 Handling "In-the-Wild" and Unconstrained Photo Collections

The canonical 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) formulation assumes a static, radiometrically consistent world, where each point in space exhibits a fixed radiance that is solely a function of viewing direction. This assumption is fundamentally violated by "in-the-wild" photo collections, such as those harvested from online databases, which aggregate images captured by numerous users under drastically varying illumination, with diverse camera post-processing pipelines, and populated by transient occluders like pedestrians or vehicles. This challenge is orthogonal yet complementary to the geometric and photometric robustness issues discussed in the previous section: whereas sparse or degraded inputs suffer from an *information deficit*, unconstrained captures suffer from *information conflicts*—the same surface is observed under inconsistent appearance and with foreign, ephemeral content, jointly obscuring the true static geometry and reflectance. Reconstructing robust and high-quality scenes from such unconstrained data necessitates a paradigm shift from modeling a single static appearance to explicitly disentangling the persistent scene structure and reflectance from ephemeral, per-image variations. The primary research thrusts can be categorized into four complementary strategies: appearance-conditioned modeling, transient-object handling, semantics-guided decomposition, and uncertainty-aware fusion.

A prominent approach to handle appearance variation is to condition the view-dependent appearance of Gaussians on a per-image latent code. Drawing inspiration from the computer graphics concept of a "tone-mapper," methods employ a per-image appearance embedding or a residual-based module that modifies the base spherical harmonic coefficients, effectively adapting each Gaussian to the specific lighting and white-balance of an input image [67]. This latent modulation allows the optimization to disentangle the canonical scene albedo from the photometric transformations of each capture, yielding a more consistent aggregate synthesis and enabling appearance transfer between views. However, the representational capacity of a single residual vector can be a limiting factor for highly complex or *non-parametric* changes in illumination, such as dynamic shadows or specular highlight changes. Therefore, more granular approaches are required to decouple appearance on a per-primitive basis, similar to how depth and normal priors are selectively and locally injected into geometry optimization in the previous section.

Another critical component in handling the "in-the-wild" setting is the isolation of transient occluders and distractors, which otherwise corrupt the optimized geometry of the static scene. Analogous to the concept of distractor handling in classical photogrammetry and recent implicit methods [68], research has integrated "mask predictors" and residual feature maps directly into the Gaussian optimization process [69]. These components are designed to learn and identify per-image inconsistencies. By predicting a mask or a weighted transiency map, the optimizer can effectively down-weight or ignore the gradients originating from transient pedestrians or vehicles, preventing them from being fused into the canonical and geometrically clean scene representation. Rather than fully discarding potentially valuable pixels—which is a known limitation in strong sparse-view regularization—some strategies aim for a more confident or consistency-driven fusion by combining information based on geometric and color reliability across observations, creating a form of robust "less-reliable observation aggregation" that parallels the uncertainty weighting discussed in depth-sensor fusion [41].

Semantic and structural priors are also increasingly leveraged to enforce consistency under variable conditions. By integrating foundation model features extracted from 2D models like SAM or CLIP into the 3D Gaussian field [69], methods facilitate semantic correspondences across images captured under vastly different times of the day or seasons. These correspondences act as robust anchors for optimizing geometry and appearance, mitigating the ambiguity introduced by the changing appearance and serving a role analogous to the MVS or depth anchors in sparse-view methods. Furthermore, architectural advances are increasingly incorporating per-Gaussian uncertainty to orchestrate which observations contribute most to the canonical model, creating a form of "confidence-aware rendering" that is directly extensible to fusion with multi-modal or multimodel depth signals.

Looking forward, the field lies at the intersection of generative and robust statistical models. Combining recent diffusion-based models as generation priors for occluded or unseen regions holds great potential to not just hallucinate but to "complete" a scene in a physically and semantically consistent way, significantly improving performance on unconstrained collections. Future research will likely pursue architectures that dynamically disentangle the latent appearance code into physically Gall meaningful properties, such as scalar illumination intensity, correlated color temperature, and a static camera response function, thereby facilitating higher-level appearance editing and physically grounded relighting. In closing, the challenge of in-the-wild 3D reconstruction is thus not only a test of geometric fidelity but also a model's ability to dynamically aggregate, weigh, and disentangle a multi-attribute world observation—an ability that will underpin the integration of dense, heterogeneous sensor inputs discussed in the next part of this survey.

### 3.5 Integration with External Sensors and Multi-Modal Depth Priors

The maturation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from a purely image-driven reconstruction framework into a versatile multi-modal scene representation paradigm hinges on its capacity to integrate external geometric cues. While photometric loss functions provide rich appearance supervision, they are fundamentally ill-posed for recovering accurate geometry in texture-less regions, under sparse view configurations, or in the presence of specularities. The integration of depth priors derived from active sensors, such as LiDAR or RGB-D cameras, and passive self-supervised monocular estimators, directly addresses this liability by funnelling explicit 3D constraints into the optimization.

A primary strategy couples 3DGS with established SLAM front-ends to jointly estimate camera pose and the Gaussian map both in the tracking and mapping iterations [53; 18]. To enhance the robustness of dense tracking, uncertainty-aware optimization frameworks have been proposed that estimate and discard unstable Gaussian primitives to favor the valuable ones for optimization without the stability tests, achieving tracking speeds up to 15 Hz and superior accuracy and mapping performance [53; 18]. However, the stability test in these integrated models is often limited, and their extension to laser-fused global frameworks remains an open frontier for large-scale simultaneity.

For the scenarios where the camera-SLAM baselines are restrictive or degenerate, the fusion of lower-frequency sensors like sound navigation and ranging is critical. In restricted underwater settings, the direct coupling of range and bearing data from sonar compensates for the deficits of sparse or missing viewpoints [53]. This synergistic fusion can directly support the reconstruction of geometrically consistent digital twins where visual features are scarce, underscoring the need for sensor-specific fusion rather than generic depth encodings.

Another powerful and accessible alternative to dedicated hardware is using learned geometric priors to regularize the 3DGS volume [35]. These losses enforce strong geometric constraints from off-shelf foundation models and are used in few-shot reconstruction pipelines [70]. Monocular priors and Spherical Harmonics activation are crucial as some high-dynamic-range specular scenes are extremely sensitive to depth map errors [22]. Its boundary coupling function robustly discards occlusions and latitude-aware checkpoints define a more general and robust deep regularization that is unsolved. A key challenge is to lock the monocular geometry and better encode the uncertainty and multi-view-instabilities into these priors, both of which are currently heavy heuristic and unsupported.

Generative priors are further funnelled into the optimization to address extreme sparsity [39]. A coarse-to-fine scheme can refine normals and patch-matching priors, mitigating over-smoothness and floaters in the absence of ground-truth geometry [70; 36]. The directional consistency in particular stabilizes the geometry-aware training and remains a fast remedy for the intrinsic high-frequency overfitting of Gaussian primitives.

Despite successes, the integration events between global depth sensors (LiDAR) and local monocular priors reveal a critical trade-off: the hard labels from LiDAR improve large-scale accuracy but do not close the data gap between high-frequency details and deformable objects. A new frontier is the decomposable scene placement of fusion of photometry + dense geometry maintained practically with spatially-varying fusion, incorporating a densification gate with pixel-adaptive weights and hierarchical continuous geometric context to lead to the trustful geometric priors, achieving both precision and cohesion. The systematic aggregation of these multi-modal cameras is the only sustainable path to truly scale 3DGS from as an offline optical rendering architecture to a complete, sampled, continuous geometrical representation.

## 4 Efficiency, Compression, and Scalability

### 4.1 Hardware-Accelerated Rendering and Rasterization Optimization

The relentless pursuit of interactive frame rates for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has positioned the tile-based differentiable rasterizer as both the enabling technology and the primary computational bottleneck of the paradigm. While the foundational work of Kerbl et al. [7] established a highly efficient GPU pipeline, its viability across diverse consumer, mobile, and embedded platforms hinges on continuous, hardware-aware algorithmic innovation. This subsection dissects the principal axes of optimization, moving from kernel-level engineering to high-level scene structure exploitation, to achieve high-fidelity rendering beyond the capabilities of the initial implementation.

A primary focus of recent research is the meticulous refinement of the GPU execution path. The original rasterizer’s per-pixel complexity, stemming from sorting and blending millions of anisotropic primitives, presents significant opportunities for improved memory access patterns and compute utilization. To address these, the `gsplat` library has emerged as a modular and highly optimized CUDA backend, introducing warp-level primitives and more efficient parallel scan operations that decouple the forward and backward passes for enhanced flexibility and reduced memory overhead. Complementing this, FlashGS [71] directly targets memory-bound bottlenecks by implementing a vectorized, tile-based pipeline that improves cache locality and atomic operation efficiency through a "flash" scheduling mechanism. Empirical results from FlashGS demonstrate substantial FPS improvements—often exceeding 4×—across a variety of datasets by minimizing the latency inherent in memory-heavy read-write operations. This low-level optimization ensures that the theoretical parallel capacity of modern GPUs is more effectively translated into hands-on rendering speed.

Beyond raw kernel efficiency, eliminating redundant computation through sophisticated culling strategies is vital, particularly for large-scale or sparsely populated scenes. The naive pipeline processes all Gaussians within a tile’s bounding box, failing to account for empty space or heavily occluded regions. Hierarchical culling mechanisms, such as occupancy grids and spatial data structures, directly address this inefficiency. Specifically, methods inspired by voxel-based acceleration, like those used in Octree-GS [52], and hierarchical culling approaches in RadSplat [8], facilitate the rapid identification and skipping of inactive or low-contribution Gaussians before the expensive per-pixel blending stage. By eliminating irrelevant work from the rendering equation, these effective pruning strategies reduce the sort list size and the computational load on the rasterization cores. This synergy between spatial indexing and the rasterizer advances scaling 3DGS to unbounded environments without compromising frame rate.

The final area of optimization is the design of the pipeline itself, specifically the formulations for sorting and blending. The original method relies on a global per-pixel sort, a costly operation that scales super-linearly with the number of primitives. Hierarchical rasterization schemes, such as those proposed in StopThePop [30], challenge this premise by introducing a hierarchical data structure that assigns a weight to the sort for improved efficiency. This design, while adding a mere 4% overhead in its baseline mode, is able to enforce view consistency when per-pixel depth is required, and by enabling a reduction in Gaussian count, it can ultimately achieve a 1.6× speedup over the original algorithm. This is complemented by algorithmic refinements in data scheduling and visibility-aware rendering that aim to make the algorithm bandwidth-bound rather than latency-bound [7]. Such holistic improvements ensure that the advanced high quality blending and level-of-detail use cases do not come at the cost of performance.

Looking towards the future, we are clearly at the frontier of fusing these optimization levels with the rapid development in AI compute. The emergence of concepts like tensor cores, and the desire to move beyond cuDA into operation which can be compiled for different platforms, suggests that more marginal returns could be achieved by leveraging level-of-detail structures and hierarchical methods [9]. The ultimate goal is an increasingly block-wise adaptive rasterizer that can reallocate compute per scene and per view, making high-fidelity, real-time 3DGS a ubiquitous reality across the digital ecosystem.

### 4.2 Model Compression, Pruning, and Storage Reduction

The inherent scalability of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is bounded by its substantial memory footprint; a single optimized scene can require hundreds of megabytes due to millions of anisotropic primitives and high-order spherical harmonic coefficients. While the preceding discussion established the algorithmic foundations of the tile-based rasterizer, the practical deployment of 3DGS across consumer, mobile, and embedded platforms—particularly when paired with the real-time optimization strategies to be examined in the following subsection—hinges critically on solving this storage bottleneck. This subsection categorizes the primary strategies for compression and storage reduction, which are essential for enabling interactive frame rates and feasible memory usage before the rendering acceleration techniques can be meaningfully applied.

**Sparsity and Importance-Based Primitive Pruning.** A direct strategy for reducing memory consumption is decreasing the primitive count. Early approaches proposed resolution-aware pruning, which selects Gaussians based on their image-space footprint to eliminate those that are unnecessarily small or redundant, achieving roughly a 2× reduction in primitives [72]. More principled methods construct a graph on Gaussian primitives to perform spectral down-sampling, pruning nodes via a high-pass graph filter while a lightweight neural head compensates for the lost high-frequency signals [73]. Similarly, the method's opacity and cache complexity have been used to prune prone-to-vacancy Gaussians [73]. Sample-based simplification, such as those used in Mini-Splatting, reframes density control as a sampling problem to achieve a constrained Gaussian count while maintaining rendering quality [19]. A comprehensive analysis from Reducing the Memory Footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting further highlights that half-float precision for attributes, alongside pruning, leads to significant memory savings, achieving about a 27× reduction for tested scenes [72]. In a similar vein, analytical approaches that introduce hierarchical sorting also prune half the Gaussians [30] during preprocessing, thereby aligning the reduced primitive count with faster rasterization in the rendering pipeline discussed later.

**Quantization and Efficient Coding.** Quantizing the high-precision floating-point values into lower-bit codes is a complementary, yet powerful, approach. A codebook-based vector quantization (VQ) method [72] learns compact codebooks for geometric attributes (scale and rotation), achieving a further storage reduction. This was more explicitly formalized in Compact 3D Gaussian (C3DGS), which combines VQ with learnable masks and grid-based alternative fields, reporting a consistent 25× storage reduction against vanilla 3DGS [27]. A key challenge for VQ is the non-uniform distribution of attributes across a scene. Recent methods [27] proposal to project the 3D Gaussians onto a self-organizing map, then quantize the co-located neural features, using quantized coordinates to enable attribute spaces to be more uniformly distributed and learned more effectively. These compact attribute representations necessitate that the subsequent rendering phase can efficiently decompose and access the decoded data; just as the previous subsection's pruning and LOD techniques removed the overhead of accessing empty regions, the algorithm-level coordination for quantized data—such as alignment with the tile-based data structures discussed in the following subsection—becomes essential for translating storage savings into actual bandwidth reduction.

**Neural and Structured Compensation.** An alternative to pruning and quantization is to remove redundancy in the parameters themselves by using compact, spatially coherent representations. The encoding of spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients can be re-parameterized into a grid-based neural field [27], reducing the per-Gaussian storage from a high-dimensional vector to a low-dimensional feature lookup, with a small MLP to decode the color. Additionally, graph-based approaches [73] deploy a post-pruning neural compensation module that learns to mix the splatted features, which fills the un-pruned areas while lowering the parameter count. Such structured designs are particularly synergistic with the hierarchical and multi-resolution anchoring strategies discussed in the next subsection, because they create a compact intermediate value and level-of-detail mechanisms that are both cache-friendly and directly usable by the rasterizer’s culling stage.

The field exhibits several key trends. The most promising line of research lies in the combination of compression strategies into a holistic pipeline and algorithm-level co-design. For example, the combined use of pruning, quantization, and neural compensation in [27; 72] demonstrates that these methods are often complementary, achieving multiplicative reductions that surpass any single technique. A second trend is the shift from heuristic, hand-crafted schemes to learned, data-driven ones, as seen in the spectral graph filtering [73] and neural compensation networks [73]. Looking ahead, future research is likely to emerge in two important areas. The first is the extension of these compression schemes to dynamic or 4D Gaussian representations, where temporal coherence presents new opportunities for removing both spatial and temporal redundancy. The second is the establishment of a rate-distortion theory for Gaussian splatting, which would allow for a principled, task-agnostic approach to optimizing the bitrate (the number of Gaussians, the quantization level, or the neural field size) against the distortion (perceptual and pixel quality) [27]. More recently, relation to storage and bandwidth constraints when combined with the LoD culling and hierarchical schemes discussed in the following subsection—where reducing the number of active, full-precision primitives inside the renderer’s view frustum reduces both the byte footprint and the per-frame rasterization cost—highlights a broader co-design trend: compression techniques that treat rendering memory and compute as interchangeable constraints [13] and that prioritize encoding efficiency before hardware-level execution will be most effective. This co-design between what is stored (compression), what is rendered (LoD selection), and how it is rasterized (GPU-scheduling) is the key to realizing the full performance envelope of 3DGS on real-time systems.

### 4.3 Level-of-Detail and Hierarchical Structures for Large-Scale Scenes

The escalating scale of captured scenes, from room-scale environments to unbounded city models comprising tens of thousands of images, presents a fundamental challenge to the resource-intensive nature of vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting. The naive approach of globally optimizing a monolithic set of Gaussian primitives becomes computationally intractable and memory-prohibitive as scene complexity grows. Hierarchical and level-of-detail (LoD) structures have emerged as the principal solution paradigm to address these scalability bottlenecks, enabling interactive frame rates and adaptive memory footprints without compromising visible fidelity.

A foundational strategy for taming large-scale scenes involves partitioning the environment into manageable, independently optimized blocks, followed by a consolidation phase. [9] presents a pioneering divide-and-conquer approach where the scene is split into chunks that are trained in parallel, then merged into a unified hierarchy. A key insight from this work is the adaption of the training procedure to handle the sparse and often overlapping coverage common in large captures, preventing overfitting and artifacts and ensuring visually coherent transitions between chunks. This two-stage approach—independent training followed by hierarchical consolidation—avoids the memory explosion associated with global optimization and establishes a robust foundation for streaming and selective rendering.

Building upon this spatial decomposition, explicit LoD frameworks have been developed to dynamically manage the level of detail based on viewing conditions. [52] introduces an LOD-structured 3D Gaussian approach that stores multi-resolution anchor points. The model dynamically selects a resolution-appropriate level of detail during rasterization, ensuring performance is less contingent on the total scene complexity and providing consistent frame rates when zooming in and out. This is achieved by using a structural hierarchy to guide where new Gaussians are placed via an efficient info-gain-guided density control. This avoids unstable training and ensures that the resulting hierarchy optimally represents the spatial distribution of the signal. This approach directly tackles the variability in the number of "active" Gaussians, shifting the rendering cost from being a function of the total scene size to being a function of the current view frustum and desired detail. The challenge remains in the design of a unified and seamless mechanism for transitioning between levels to prevent popping artifacts. This is accomplished by enforcing consistent representation of the same signal across levels and using extra regularization to ensure smooth crossfades between levels.

In contrast to per-object or per-block LoD, more recent approaches like [74] and [75] address the concept of level-of-detail from a signal-processing perspective. They focus on the fundamental cause of scale-dependent aliasing, [74] showing that a mismatch between the sampling frequency of the target view and the spatial frequency of the 3D Gaussians causes the problem.
