### 7.1 Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) and Dense Scene Reconstruction

The integration of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems marks a paradigm shift in dense visual perception, transitioning from purely geometric reconstructions to photorealistic, differentiable scene representations that are jointly optimized with camera trajectories. This subsection examines how the explicit, point-based structure of 3DGS is uniquely suited for real-time SLAM, enabling dense geometry estimation, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis, and robust tracking within a unified framework. The survey by [18] traces the evolutionary trajectory from classical hand-crafted methods through deep learning-based approaches to the current radiance-field era, observing that discrete point representations have achieved a role analogous to landmarks used in classical visual odometry while producing continuous, differentiable maps.

The central stream of research addresses dense tracking and mapping for RGB-D sensors. Differentiable rendering of Gaussian maps facilitates the joint estimation of camera pose and map parameters by minimizing photometric and geometric residuals simultaneously. To this end, joint optical flow and depth are estimated using a direct approach that optimizes the Gaussian map and poses. In a closely related approach, a compact and fast trainable 3D Gaussian map is used to jointly optimize camera pose and map parameters, with several designed to prune and clone Gaussians to maintain a low number of primitives while ensuring colour and depth consistency. These methods also exploit the differentiable rasterizer that differs from the original implementation by optimizing the covariance of the Gausssians to enable accurate dense geometry reconstruction and structure-aware map optimization. This progress is significant as, unlike earlier NeRF-based SLAM, these systems allow real-time tracking that matches or exceeds traditional visual odometry.

A major open challenge is long-term drift in large trajectories and loop detection. To address this, loop closure and submap registration are introduced, with a method that aligns 3D Gaussian submaps when a loop is detected using pose graph optimization to maintain global consistency. This effectively re-establishes the correct geometry and avoids the accumulation of errors over time. This strategy is advantageous compared to NeRF-based SLAM, where global loop closure is challenging due to a lack of registerable geometry or effective optimization without local minima.

Extensions beyond dense RGB-D have also been made into monocular systems. In such systems, the process relies on input poses estimated from a virtual odometry, and depth maps are estimated from monocular cues to anchor sparse inputs, making the existing robust system applicable in scenarios without a depth sensor. Upcoming work includes multimodal systems that combine semantic understanding with Gaussian representations [109]. Such hybrid systems may provide reliable localization, mapping, and semantic understanding, forming the basis for a robust next generation of robots.

These methods use the 3D Gaussian Splatting as a differentiable ray-casting representation without any surface regularizers; the map’s implicit smoothing of the uncertainty in pose and geometry is generated directly from the covariance of the Gaussian. For example, state-of-the-art methods show that a Scene Model that jointly infers uncertainties of both pose and the scene is able to distill depth noise into the covariances of the map points, leading to better tracking robustness. In summary, applying physics-based priors to the Gaussian map, such as local rigidity, or building a system with temporal configuration is fully capable of controlling scale beyond rendering practice. Yet, there remain limitations of Gaussian SLAM in dynamic and large-scale environments: using the Gaussian representation maintains mostly static scenes while being computationally limited; standard SGD optimization of the Gaussian is not designed for the large 3D base maps; the failure to prioritize memory before temporal robustness and incremental adaptation to the dynamic world, and the unprincipled mapping of uncertainty. Future 3DGS-SLAM systems may, therefore, be able to integrate models from recent dynamic work [13; 14], physical underlying constraints [46; 23], and make use of multi-modal data [109] to solve these challenging tasks. More broadly, the model remains tenable as a core backbone for a 4D world model; not only to reconstruct a single moment but to continuously stream, predict, and alter the 3D scenes—bridging dense image understanding and robot autonomy.

### 7.2 Robotics, Autonomous Navigation, and Physical Simulation

The integration of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into robotics and physical simulation represents a paradigm shift from passive scene reconstruction toward actionable, closed-loop perception-action systems. While the previous subsection established 3DGS as a powerful tool for dense visual perception in SLAM, this subsection examines how the explicit, point-based structure of Gaussian primitives—which enables direct manipulation and analysis—positions them as an ideal substrate for physical simulation and robotic interaction. Unlike implicit neural radiance fields that require expensive volumetric sampling for each query, the explicit formulation of Gaussian kernels allows for seamless integration with physics engines, turning the representation from a purely appearance-based geometry into a unified framework for both rendering and predictive dynamics. This expansion from visual perception to physical AI naturally complements the trajectory of Gaussian-based SLAM established earlier, while providing the structured, manipulable scene substrate that the semantic and language grounding discussed in the following subsection will build upon to deliver interactive and intelligent 3D systems.

The integration of physics into Gaussian representations has been explored through a unified framework where 3D Gaussian kernels are equipped with physically meaningful kinematic deformation and mechanical stress attributes, evolving in accordance with continuum mechanics principles. Notably, in [33], the Material Point Method is seamlessly integrated with the Gaussian representation such that the same primitives serve as the discrete representation for both physical simulation and visual rendering. This exemplifies the principle of *what you see is what you simulate*, negating the need for triangle meshing, marching cubes, or geometric embedding, and enabling high-quality synthesis of novel motions for a variety of materials including elastic entities, metals, non-Newtonian fluids, and granular materials. This tight coupling between rendering and simulation is also reflected in the work on Gaussian Splashing [23], which integrates position-based dynamics with 3D Gaussian kernels to synthesize dynamic fluids. By enhancing the Gaussian kernels with surface normals to refine particle-based simulations, this approach eliminates spiky artifacts and enables correct physical cues for fluid behavior from novel views. Obtaining realistic physical descriptions of elastic objects with Spring-Mass 3D Gaussians [110] similarly integrates a 3D Spring-Mass model into the Gaussian kernel, allowing for the reconstruction, from multiple-view videos, of the visual appearance, shape, and physical dynamics of elastic objects, offering accurate prediction of future deformation states based on different initial configurations.

Beyond simulation, the explicit structure of Gaussian Splatting is a supportive substrate for robotics perception. A novel dual Gaussian-Particle representation was developed to model the physical world in a real-time correctable manner, combining the geometric support of particles with visual rendering of attached 3D Gaussians [25]. This world model allows predictive physics simulation while simultaneously performing online corrections from image observations. By comparing predicted and observed renders, the system computes corrective visual forces that guide particle positions to adhere to physical constraints for continuous real-time synchronization with the environment while remaining consistent with the underlying physics. Operating at 30Hz using only three cameras, this system demonstrates the unique capability of 3DGS to model static, photorealistic scenes while also serving as a policy backbone for embodied agents interacting with environments. The potential of Gaussian-based world models for large-scale autonomous systems is supported by work on very large scenes, which presents a hierarchy of 3D Gaussians that allows real-time rendering while preserving visual quality, with capture trajectories of up to several kilometers [30]. This viewpoint makes 3DGS an attractive component in a real-time rendering stack that requires access to compact and faithful representations.

When used for a higher-level objective, such as robotic manipulation, the explicit nature of the Gaussians allows one to directly segment points and visual semantics relevant to grasping, path-planning, and interaction primitives. Recent work extends 3DGS with a compact Identity Encoding, allowing the Gaussian primitives to be partitioned, tracked, and edited according to arbitrary levels of detail [11]. This enables flexible object removal, inpainting, colorization, and re-composition via user-defined 2D masks, establishing an axiomatic link among geometric structure, visual appearance, and editable semantics—an architecture that is particularly advantageous for fine-grained scene manipulation and object-level reasoning. Moreover, dynamic reconstruction frameworks such as MoSca [111] couple a motion scaffold with an underlying Gaussian scene representation, providing robust correspondences between video evidence and the motion scaffold over time, which are essential for accurate robotic perception in human-centric unconstrained environments. Collectively, these works show that 3DGS emerges as a key enabler for the next generation of 3D world simulators — the basis for generative formats of physical AI, where the ability to virtually interact, physically simulate, and semantically reason over a scene is as important as the photometric fidelity. While the static scene assumption persists in several SLAM systems described previously, the integration of physics and dynamic modeling presented here overcomes these constraints, unlocking the path forward to the seamless injection of semantic features and linguistic reasoning into dynamic and interactive Gaussian world models that the following section will describe. Rather than remaining an appearance-centric geometry representation, Gaussian Splatting is thus expanding into the broader discipline of 4D world modeling, where continuous simulation and real-time correctability create the backbone for both robot autonomy and human-centric interactive applications.

### 7.3 Language-Embedded and Semantic Scene Understanding

The integration of language and semantic understanding into 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a paradigm shift from purely photometric scene reconstruction toward holistic, queryable 3D representations. Unlike implicit neural radiance fields, whose continuous nature complicates feature attachment, the explicit, discrete structure of Gaussian primitives offers a natural substrate for embedding dense, multi-modal semantic features. This subsection critically examines the methodologies for distilling vision-language features into 3DGS, exploring the mechanisms of feature embedding, representation strategies for scalability, and the synergistic integration of large language models (LLMs) for interactive reasoning. The overarching goal is to move beyond mere object identification towards a comprehensive understanding of *what* objects are and *what they are*, enabling open-vocabulary querying, fine-grained segmentation, and grounded reasoning within the reconstructed scene.

The dominant paradigm for language grounding is semantic feature distillation, which transfers high-dimensional features from pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) into the 3D Gaussian field. The foundational challenge here is reconciling the spatial and channel inconsistencies between high-resolution RGB images and the lower-resolution, often spatially coarse, feature maps from models like CLIP or SAM. Techniques such as Feature 3DGS [103] have introduced architectural and training changes to efficiently distill features from state-of-the-art 2D foundation models directly into the per-Gaussian attributes. This enables a suite of downstream tasks, including novel view semantic segmentation, language-guided editing, and "Segment Anything" through explicit prompting. The choice of VLM significantly influences the semantic quality: CLIP-derived features offer excellent textual alignment suitable for open-vocabulary classification, while SAM-derived features provide superior instance-level boundaries for precise segmentation. This representation, however, is not without trade-offs. High-dimensional feature vectors drastically increase the memory footprint per primitive, and naïve concatenation can lead to color-feature interference. Subsequent works have sought to mitigate this via compact, learned feature decoders that map lower-dimensional representations to the target space, balancing fidelity against memory consumption.

Beyond distillation, a significant thrust is transitioning from scene-specific models to generalizable, open-vocabulary semantic fields. Rather than overfitting to a single scene, these methods aim to create models that can understand semantics from any new 3DGS representation at training or inference time. This direction tackles the challenge of semantic taxonomy, departing from the fixed category labels of closed-set benchmarks. For instance, comprehensive benchmarks are emerging to evaluate and train models that not only classify objects but also predict fine-grained linguistic attributes—affordances, materials, and function [26; 29]. This highlights a movement toward comprehensive semantic understanding, where the 3D representation is becoming a robust substrate for grounding abstract knowledge in a spatial context.

More recent research has been breaking down the boundaries between the explicit Gaussian primitives, LLMs, and robotic or interactive systems to achieve targeted scene understanding. By integrating a 3D Gaussian field with a Large Language Model, we can deploy contextual-aware canonical phrases to realize zero-shot segmentation. A key innovation is the introduction of *referent tokens*, which are learnable query vectors that bridge the 3DGS representation, the LLM, and lower-level vision models. This setup improves the robust grounding of objects from ambiguous natural language. This level of integration allows the system to understand the spatial reasoning of 3D scenes. This extends to the domain of interactive robot perception, where the "semantically anchored" reasoning leads to more complex reasoning and text-grounded manipulation capabilities.

Ultimately, semantic embedding represents a foundational step toward creating a unified, interactive framework. The choice of the Gaussian kernel model for this underlying semantic scene is not simply a base but a structured representation that may interact with neural networks [60]. By distilling language features and connecting them to LLMs, those techniques enable editing and parameterization of the environment. This creates a 3D scene that can be queried, segmented, verbalized, and even transformed using high-level linguistic descriptions, which overcomes the bottleneck of static photometry, and steps into the era of machine comprehension of three-dimensional environments.

### 7.4 VR/AR, Interactive Editing, and Real-Time Visualization

The convergence of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with immersive technologies marks a paradigm shift in how virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR) environments are captured, transmitted, and interacted with. Building directly upon the semantic embedding and language-grounded querying capabilities introduced earlier, the explicit, point-based nature of the representation provides a unique bridge between photorealistic fidelity and the strict computational, memory, and latency budgets inherent to head-mounted displays (HMDs) and edge devices—transforming the now-queryable 3D scene into a manipulable and interactive medium. In conventional VR/AR pipelines, the creation of interactive scenes is bifurcated: one path prioritizes high-fidelity offline rendering at the cost of interactivity, while the other favors lightweight, but visually simplistic, polygon-based models. 3DGS directly addresses this dichotomy, extending the semantic queryability from the prior section into a dual role: it serves simultaneously as a high-fidelity radiance field, a manipulable point cloud, and a rasterization-ready primitive set, enabling streaming detail and in-place, language-guided editing without compromising frame rate—functional demands that arise naturally from the semantic understanding achieved through feature distillation and LLM grounding established above.

A primary challenge for content streaming arises from transmission bandwidth, particularly when moving from the single-scene, language-anchored representations discussed previously to distributed and remote rendering systems. A single, overfitted scene can contain millions of Gaussian primitives, representing hundreds of megabytes of data, rendering it impractical for standard wireless transmission to the resource-constrained HMDs. Contemporary methodologies tackle this through simplified, device-adaptive paradigms that maintain the semantic cohesiveness introduced earlier. Approaches such as Mini-Splatting [19] reorganize the spatial distribution of Gaussians via blur splitting and depth reinitialization to represent scenes with a constrained primitive count. This is complemented by level-of-detail (LoD) structures that allow the culling of far-field primitives while preserving the dense feature fields required for open-vocabulary understanding on-edge. Crucially, these compression strategies must operate under a rate-distortion trade-off specific to remote rendering scenarios, where the goal is not merely to reduce file size but to reduce the *per-frame* bitrate delivered to the GPU. Compression via spectral pruning and neural compensation [73] demonstrates that a lightweight MLP network head can mix a primal, selected set of splatted Gaussian features to compensate for quality losses, creating a linked representation where the "latent" state of the field—the true mapping between primitives and the MLP—can be compressed for transmission, ensuring that high-level semantic grounding is preserved without exhausting bandwidth budgets.

Beyond static fidelity, this tight coupling of the representation to interactive physics and direct manipulation resolves historical challenges of editing digital content. Where NeRF-based offline rendering requires significant compute per update, 3DGS facilitates direct parameter editing of geometric primitives—a capability enhanced by the semantic anchoring from the previous section, which provides practical affordances for real-time aesthetic changes to object translation, removal, and transfer [112], as well as feature-level manipulation to achieve novel effects [103]. The explicit query-ability established via the language-aware features extends seamlessly into immersive interactions. By distilling semantic features from 2D foundation models (e.g., CLIP, SAM) into these volumes, semantic fields are established, enabling direct manipulation of objects sampled by a single point or bounding box [103]. This capability integrates smoothly with diffusion models, where natural language instructions can be used to iteratively edit the visual appearance of the whole scene, transporting the high-level semantic control from the prior section into a visual and immersive arena, and ushering in a new era of casual user interaction with the 3D world, bypassing specialized graphics tools for semantic and text-guided pipelines [67; 100].

This realism and robust interactivity gain further traction when considering the distantly handled case of low-quality, insufficiently textured inputs. Realistic and robust interaction within the reconstruction of broader, unbounded scenes depends on precise geometry. On real-time mobile devices, the lack of accurate geometry initialization severely degrades optimization. This is addressed by integrating Structure-from-Motion (SfM) priors within Gaussian-based SLAM frameworks, where the robust sparse initialization from SfM is coupled with the inherent strength of the primitives for local reconstruction—preserving the fidelity required for tracking and interaction. Furthermore, introducing optical flow awareness into the splatting representation—as done by [113]—improves geometry for complex or sparse motion cases, which is crucial for the interplay between real-time tracking and low-memory consumption on edge devices. Despite these advances, the bottleneck of splatting-based immersive rendering remains asynchronous I/O and texture utilization, where mobile devices experience compression and latency in the suboptimal graphics pipeline of HMDs. The explicit representation’s strength in ease of manipulationwhile facilitating interactive language-guided and physics-driven editing as shown above-exists within a context that necessitates new forms of constrained transmission and sparse parameter transport to maintain a minimum latency loop that satisfies the real-time demands of VR/AR and the computational suite of autonomous systems discussed in the following subsection.

The path forward lies in the synthesis of physical priors with rate-aware primitives, fostering a natural transition from the semantic interactivity of this section to the highly specialized, scaled applications of the next. We anticipate a trend where head-mounted 3DGS will be coupled with dynamic scene decompositionas perfected in the following section's autonomous drivingand event-driven and neuromorphic rendering, shifting focus from "universal load" to "sparse or local load" editing. The promise of 3DGS in this domain is double-sided: the point-based representation becomes a bridge, being at once the medium for interactive physics simulations and the carrier of global illumination. Interactive networks in future architectures must be trained to compress the 3D hierarchy, with direct access from interacting modules for 3D dynamic editing, rather than solely accessing the viewing parameters, offering a competitive new cornerstone for communication and interaction with the scene format. This sets the stage for the re-evaluation of the core assumptions of static geometry and optical fidelity, as fundamentally distinct, high-stakes, transformative-and demanding-applications (urban modeling, surgical robotics, and tomographic vision) push the framework to incorporate robust 4D dynamics and physical plausibility, as the following subsection dissects in depth.

### 7.5 Specialised Domains and Scientific Imaging (Autonomous Driving, Medical, and Tomography)

The deployment of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in specialised, high-impact domains necessitates a fundamental re-evaluation of its core assumptions—namely, static geometry, optically transparent media, and a well-conditioned camera model. While the base representation excels in object-centric and bounded scenes, autonomous driving, surgical robotics, and tomographic imaging present unique constraints ranging from extreme scale and dynamic object decomposition to the physics of non-visible radiation and highly deformable tissues. This subsection explores how the core 3DGS framework is being systematically adapted to satisfy the accuracy, robustness, and real-time requirements of these demanding application areas.

A primary challenge is modeling unbounded, dynamic urban environments from a monocular rig. An early representation, Street Gaussians [114], addressed this by decomposing the scene into a set of point clouds with semantic logits and 3D Gaussians, each associated with either a foreground vehicle or the static background. This explicit decomposition allows for the learning of optimizable tracked poses and dynamic appearance models for each object, enabling photorealistic novel view synthesis and scene editing operations with high quality. This segmentation is fundamental for creating realistic and interactive simulations. Building upon this, HUGS [115] formulates a joint optimization problem for geometry, appearance, semantics, and motion over a combination of static and dynamic Gaussians, producing a holistic urban representation that facilitates downstream tasks like semantic segmentation and object tracking. The efficacy of these models, however, is often limited by their reliance on accurate tracked object poses, motivating continued research into more robust, self-supervised 4D decompositions. These advances are the pivotal step for autonomous driving, enabling not only photorealistic sensor simulation but also a deeper
semantic and geometric understanding of the surrounding world for navigation and planning.

In the medical sphere, the limitations of structure-from-motion in texture-poor environments dictate bespoke solutions. Given that endoscopic scenes in minimally invasive surgery are highly deformable, have significant specularities, and lack reliable SfM initialization, methods are explicitly designed to circumvent these failures. LGS [116] provides a representation designed to meet the real-time and compute constraints of surgical environments. By integrating deformation-aware pruning and feature field condensation, it minimizes redundant Gaussian quantities and attributes, thereby enabling a reduction in memory consumption while maintaining high visual fidelity for deformable tissue reconstruction. Further, in the limited frame-rate computation and reliance on monocular captures from a single endoscope, the ability of splatting-based methods to render only relevant components without sacrificing speed is critical. These methods serve as a powerful testament to the adaptability of the representation when the prior constraints of static cameras and sufficient texture are removed, signifying a promising avenue for guidance systems and surgical training in robotic surgery.

Beyond optical sensing, a more radical shift entails adapting the Gaussian kernel to the physics of invisible radiation, underlining its versatility beyond conventional imaging. The complexities inherent in medical image data (such as background noise and distortions) can be addressed by this representation. For domains like precise and inverse rendering, the challenge lies in direct reconstruction of volumetric data and, crucially, the ability to efficiently understand the underlying data generation process. Since the problem consists of recovering 3D volumes from 2D projections and performing reconstruction in complex, high-motion scenarios, the conventional assumptions fall short. Instead, these methods use a bespoke approach (e.g., Gaussian splatting with a unique formulation) that cannot be collapsed into shallow multi-layer perceptrons and optimizations. They require the regrouping of a set of Gaussian kernels and the deformable-body structure of the scene to get a faithful solution that can be rendered in real-time. The generative nature of this representation allows for rendering to run at interactive
rates, but the principal factors are the design and implementation of the underlying differentiable rasterization pipeline and the capacity to be tuned for different physics.

Across these disparate applications, a critical synthesis emerges: the Gaussian primitives at the core of 3DGS are not simply a rendering tool but a versatile, differentiable data structure. Their explicit nature enables the 3D reconstructions and semantic compositions, providing a efficient alternative to NeRF-based representations. Looking forward, we expect a convergence of these methodologies. For example, techniques from medical domain—such as handling unreliable poses and deformable objects—are directly transferable to autonomous driving in complex, dynamic traffic situations, while physics-integrated, efficiency-first Gaussian representation will see a more pronounced focus on geometric fidelity and topological consistency. This frontier is not just about extending an	algorithm to new tasks but solidifying the shift of 3DGS from a tool for image synthesis to a core representational foundation for 3D scene understanding and dynamic modelling across scientific and engineering practice.

## 8 Conclusion and Future Research Directions

This survey has charted the rapid evolution of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from a novel differentiable rendering algorithm [7] to a foundational technology driving innovation across computer graphics, vision, and robotics. As we conclude, we synthesize the technological progress that has positioned 3DGS as a cornerstone of modern scene representation while identifying the complex challenges and promising opportunities that lie ahead. The journey from point-based rendering [5; 28; 6] to sparse voxel grids [1; 3] and coordinate-based networks [2] has cumulated in a representation that offers an unprecedented combination of photorealistic rendering speed, editability, and adaptability. The methodological advances in adaptive density control [41; 19], regularization [45; 46; 60; 46], and compression [27; 66; 72] have collectively expanded the capacity and robustness of the base framework, enabling applications as diverse as surface mesh extraction [117; 37; 69] and high-frequency appearance modeling [45; 65]. This synthesis reveals a field in a state of healthy, rapid maturation, yet several deep-seated questions remain.

A critical disconnect persists between the empirical efficacy of 3DGS and a mature theoretical understanding of its behavior. While the representational capacity of millions of anisotropic Gaussians is intuitively clear [7], a formal framework for analyzing its expressiveness, generalization bounds, and spectral properties remains absent. This lack of theory impedes principled, rather than heuristic, solutions to open problems. For example, the canonical issues of early over-reconstruction, gradient collisions [41], and the suboptimal spatial distribution of Gaussians [19] have all been addressed via empirical, albeit effective, heuristics. Similarly, SfM initialization [45]—a brittle dependency—and the manifold difficulties in handling sparse or degraded inputs [45; 65] highlight the need for a more principled approach to optimization and regularization. As the representation scales from single objects to unbounded, city-scale scenes [9; 114], the coherence of these point clouds will become an even more pressing issue. We posit that future research must move beyond empirical refinement and begin to develop a statistical understanding of the representation to guide densification, constraint, and regularization algorithms in a more systematic manner.

A set of significant challenge is the robustness of 3DGS in the face of unconstrained, real-world conditions. While the base model excels with well-conditioned, dense-capture inputs, its performance degrades when the input is sparse [45], blurry [65], or contains transient occluders [93]. The success of prior-based methods, particularly those integrating monocular depth and normal priors [46], and generative models for inpainting [99], demonstrates a clear direction: integrating large-scale training data with the optimization process. Future frameworks should seamlessly fuse data-driven priors with the physics-based, per-instance optimization of Gaussian splats to enforce global semantic and photometric consistency. The coupled problem of geometry and appearance optimization is particularly acute; the “Murphys’ law” of inverse specific rendering—where the optimizer might explain specular reflections as a textured surface—remains a fundamental challenge for 3D structure from images. Achieving robust and physically faithful decomposition of geometry, material, and lighting [45; 46; 118] is not just a performance issue; it is a prerequisite for the practical deployment of 3DGS in demanding fields such as facial digital twins, embedded digital twins, and the digital reconstruction of virtual environments.

The performance bottleneck has gradually shifted from rendering speed to the front-end of storage and training cost. While rendering has reached a speed of 700+ FPS for static scenes, the storage and memory footprint of millions of Gaussians remains grossly disproportionate. Compression methods [66; 27; 119] provide efficient codecs, but they often trade off quality or require an expensive offline optimization. A unifying perspective is to think of 3DGS as a data type; future work should aim to compress a full further, perhaps by sharing instance-level patterns across scenes or by learning a lower-dimensional latent space. For dynamic scenes, the explosion of data is even more significant. While deformation-based methods [46] provide elegant solutions for continuous motion, they still struggle with sudden, narratively- and structural-changing movements and long sequences. Compact and lossless representations, perhaps through a hierarchical structure for both static and dynamic, will be crucial for practical deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

Our survey also reveals a glaring standardization gap in the evaluation of performance benchmarks. The community's over-reliance on synthetic datasets like the ones from previous work [1; 3] and a handful of object-centric captures like the [1] does not capture the robust fields "in-the-wild" nature. This heterogeneity is often selectively reported, leading to a fragile underst of the field. We advocate for a comprehensive evaluation on a split of scenes, separating "geometry-based" and "appearance-based" tasks, and further include a 'cross-dataset' split to truly assess generalization. These benchmarks should consider and incorporate uncertainty, such that a model that is confident in a prediction is prized, rather than a model that is certain. Unfair and naive training-vs-quality trade-offs, where one method is trained on a curated high-res dataset and the other on a video of first-lifetime, are a challenge that must be avoided.

The future of 3DGS lies in bridging its explicit geometry with the semantic and physical world. The field is trending toward a multi-layered world where geometry, semantics [11] and physical law coexist in a holistic representation. We envision a framework where 3DGS does not exist as a unique representation but as a core "rendering-and-interaction" layer that can be trained with differentiable physics, with language for grounding, and with actions for intelligent, real-time system. The next step will be toward 3D foundations—where Gaussians are not just a goal in themselves but a means to an end, deployed across modalities to analyze, simulate, and predict physical world dynamics. The integration of physically embodied agents [46] and human-centered avatars [24] within the Gaussian framework represents a frontier for this representation, enabling a new generation of interactive 4D world models. More than just a rendering engine, 3DGS is becoming a de facto computational unit for real-time and interactive world from multi-modal inputs. As the field advances and it makes a profound impact on computer vision, it will also bring along with it questions about efficiency, robustness, and governance, and it is our hope that this survey has a graph to the way.
